When creating a post, give users the option to label it within constrained categories. Give each category a color and allow users to easily filter their searches via color coding.

On a subverse-based level, this functionality is already in place by using flairs. Flairs are tags you can put on certain posts to distinguish posts from one another. The ability to sort by flair, though, is still awaiting implementation.

On a sitewide level, on the other hand, this functionality is impossible at worst and messy at best. Since the front page is made up of a variety of subverses on different topics, styles, cultures, and ideas, who's going to decide what a category is? If you just aggregate the categories from all subscribed subverses, then what's stopping the category list from flooding five times the length of the page? How exactly does this type of functionality benefit the system more than flairs already do?

That's where I couldn't come to a conclusion. Forced labeling wouldn't be good, but I tried to pick categories that could be applied to almost any topic. Got something that shouldn't be seen by a minor? Red. Need something? Got a question? Yellow. Mod wants to post something? Purple. Want to talk about a personal issue without being mistreated? Blue. Something something? Orange. These categories could obviously use heavy revision, but as it is, Reddit already uses red for "NSFW".

As for flairs, I never paid attention to them on Reddit and another chunk of text just blends in with everything else on the page. I thought a color coded platform would be great because even the stupidest person could learn to associate certain colors with certain topics. Also, this may help users avoid misunderstanding titles.

If this was implemented, most users would likely notice the color before reading the entire title. Reading title after title gets annoying when I just want to scroll through and obtain certain types of information. If i'm drunk, i'm probably going to filter out the serious stuff. If i'm looking for a quick wank, I can click my mouse once and i'm ready. This also could be implemented for an enhanced mobile experience.

But what about if someone has a serious question? Would we allow at least 2 categories? What if someone wants to seriously ask about their yeast infection by providing pics? 3 Colors?! Perhaps the only way of doing this would be to chose categories that contrast each other.

When people communicate online, they only see text. Body language is completely lost. If visuals could be properly implemented, perhaps we could communicate a bit more effectively?

That's where I couldn't come to a conclusion. Forced labeling wouldn't be good, but I tried to pick categories that could be applied to almost any topic. [...] These categories could obviously use heavy revision, but as it is, Reddit already uses red for "NSFW".

The problem isn't revision so much than it is how any categorization system fundamentally works. First of all, the first problem is a sitewide implementation. Is the demand for such a feature high enough to put work into to implement? Would this feature be acceptable to those who dislike the idea? Even if the feature is in high demand to direct resources to, it may have to be an optional feature so others who abhor such a system could still browse the site without categories. You'd have to further develop the feature not to be too hard-coded into the site to be optional.

The second problem is how categories will be selected. Websites with categorization systems, like online stores like Amazon, sort categories by more categories; a tier system. On the surface, there are only a few categories, like Furniture, Electronics, Food, etc., but, when you enter into any category, each get more specific, like Electronics: Computers, MP3 Players, Home Entertainment, etc. Second-tier categories, like MP3 Players, aren't visible to clutter the menu on the first menu level. Hell, Amazon itself could be considered a category of Online Shopping.

Sites like Voat, on the other hand, can't be put into a category. You can have posts ranging from pointing to documentaries to announcing sick deals in your country's chain store to asking advice on building a PC. The sheer amount of categories needed to cover all of these topics could be overwhelming.

Categories are in place to differentiate content on the same level. For example, you can't place a category of 'Picture' in 'Pornography' on the same level as 'Picture' in 'Pocket Knife Request', because you'd need to explain the differentiation. Pornography's Picture category is for sorting by porn pics, while Pocket Knife Request's Picture category is used to differentiate posts from having an aiding picture alongside of it and those that don't. Their respective categories would probably look like this:

Media > Consumer > Adult > Pornography > Picture (picture of pornography)

Community > Products > Exchange > Request > Pocket Knife > Picture (posts with pictures)

Both categories have the same name, but, in different contexts, they mean completely different things. Therefore, it would be virtually impossible to create categories to sort enough content to be worth it. You may have categories that generally catch 80% of the content on the site, but you're still leaving out the 20% who feel unfairly treated that they don't get categories. If you choose to please them by adding their choice of categories, it will, again, just flood the category pool to make the system unuseable.

If you choose to categorize by methods similar to online stores' tier systems, where specific categories are sorted by their own categories or even by subverse, again, this functionality is already implemented by flairs.

As for flairs, I never paid attention to them on Reddit and another chunk of text just blends in with everything else on the page. I thought a color coded platform would be great because even the stupidest person could learn to associate certain colors with certain topics. Also, this may help users avoid misunderstanding titles.

This is not a problem caused by flairs themselves, but how moderators distinguish individual flairs. For example, my plain flairs on /v/seriousdiscussion can be easily ignored as "another chunk of text", whereas my color-coded flairs on /v/customizingvoat act to properly distinguish content types. Flairs can be used in the way you like; they just need to do so by the subverse moderators themselves.

I believe that my main point still stands, that "this functionality is impossible at worst and messy at best." There is no good way to implement categories without adding massive complications in Voat's systems and community and your idea's general functionality can already be solved by flairs.
